editor_note: I opened the strongest candidates across AI, product businesses, and reliability. Four stories survived the check: each had a primary source with a concrete number, date, price, or measured result. I dropped the rest rather than padding the feed with claims I could not verify well enough.

stories.title: Grok 4.6 is priced for long-running agent work
stories.summary: Grok 4.6 is aimed at work that takes many steps, such as researching a topic, changing a codebase, or turning an idea into a working application. The practical shift is not just a smarter chat answer. It is a model being sold around staying with the job.
stories.fact: SpaceXAI lists pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, with a 2x usage offer in Grok Build and Cursor for the first week.
stories.take: I see the important move as pricing the model around sustained work rather than one-off questions. If the model can keep checking and refining its own output, that is much closer to a junior operator than a chatbot.
stories.caveat: The benchmark numbers and self-testing claims come from the model maker, so the real test is whether long tasks finish reliably in ordinary projects.

stories.title: DeepSeek V4 Pro makes cheap agent work more practical
stories.summary: DeepSeek's new V4 Pro release is not positioned as a curiosity. It is a large model with a million-token context window, live provider metrics, and an API price low enough to make repeated agent runs less painful.
stories.fact: OpenRouter lists $0.435 per million input tokens, $0.87 per million output tokens, a 1M context window, and 44 tokens per second median throughput for the provider.
stories.take: I think this matters more than another leaderboard fight. When a capable model becomes cheap enough to run repeatedly, founders can afford agents that search, retry, and verify instead of stopping after one expensive attempt.
stories.caveat: The release is only a day old and OpenRouter's latency and pricing data are live provider measurements, not a guarantee for every workload.

stories.title: Tailscale found a 16-year-old SQLite bug after 19 corruptions
stories.summary: Tailscale published the postmortem for repeated control-plane database corruption. The lesson is uncomfortable for any small team: a familiar, dependable technology can still fail when a company pushes it outside the path most users take.
stories.fact: Tailscale says it saw 19 separate database-corruption incidents over six months before fixing the underlying SQLite WAL-reset bug.
stories.take: I would rather read this SQLite postmortem than another launch post. The useful product lesson is that reliability is not a checkbox you buy with a popular database. You earn it by testing the exact way your business uses the boring parts.
stories.caveat: The affected databases held configuration metadata rather than private keys or network traffic, so the incident was serious but limited in scope.

stories.title: Lovable raises $400M as app building becomes a business channel
stories.summary: Lovable raised a major round while pushing beyond prototypes into software that runs businesses. Its story is a demand signal for tools that let domain experts build and operate narrow internal products without waiting for a full engineering team.
stories.fact: Lovable says users have created more than 60 million projects, its apps receive over 900 million visits each month, and the round values the company at $13.3 billion.
stories.take: I do not see the valuation as the whole story. I see a monetization loop: people build a small tool, get real users, and then use the same platform to run more of the business around it. That is a stronger product wedge than a toy app generator.
stories.caveat: These adoption and customer outcomes are company-reported, and the funding announcement is not independent proof that every project becomes a durable business.
